passage: On the morning of which I speak the wind had abated, and all Nature was newly washed and fresh. It was impossible to work upon so delightful a day, and I strolled out before breakfast to enjoy the exquisite air.
rule: 'Abated' means died down. The day is 'delightful' and the air is 'newly washed and fresh', so the wind had eased.

why: Passage gives no real clue to which strength is meant; only polarity from 'respect'.
'More adroit' could equally be meticulous or diligent; the passage does not separate skill from care.

passage: After leaving the house he discovered his loss and hurried back, but found the police already in possession, owing to his own folly in leaving the candle burning. He had to pretend to be drunk in order to allay the suspicions which might have been aroused by his appearance at the gate. Now put yourself in that man’s place.
rule: 'Allay' means to calm or put to rest. He pretended to be drunk so that the suspicions 'which might have been aroused' would fade instead of grow.

passage: I confess that I had my doubts myself when I reflected upon the great traffic which had passed along the London road in the interval. My fears were soon appeased, however. Toby never hesitated or swerved, but waddled on in his peculiar rolling fashion.
rule: 'Appeased' means calmed. The word 'however' flips the mood, and 'Toby never hesitated or swerved' shows there was nothing left to fear.

passage: So furious was he that he was hardly articulate, and when he did speak it was in a much broader and more Western dialect than any which we had heard from him in the morning.

definitions.articulate: able to speak clearly and fluently

rule: 'Articulate' means able to speak clearly. He was 'so furious' that he could barely form words, and the next clause says 'when he did speak' he sounded different.

passage: I am aware that Adelbert, that my fiancé, has had a stormy life in which he has incurred bitter hatreds and most unjust aspersions. You are only the last of a series who have brought their slanders before me.

definitions.aspersions: damaging, often false remarks about someone
definitions.subterfuges: sneaky tricks to hide the truth

rule: 'Aspersions' are false, damaging remarks. The next sentence calls them 'slanders' and the first sentence calls them 'most unjust'.
why: cut after the blind test

passage: The prize-fighter, a heavily built young man with a stupid, obstinate, slab-sided face, stood awkwardly at the door, looking about him with a puzzled expression. Holmes's debonair manner was a new experience, and though he vaguely felt that it was hostile, he did not know how to counter it. He turned to his more astute comrade for help.
rule: 'Astute' means sharp and clever. The fighter has a 'stupid' face and a 'puzzled expression', so he turns to the 'more' clever partner 'for help'.

passage: Mr. Sherlock Holmes listened with attention to the long report which I was able to present to him that evening, but it did not elicit that word of curt praise which I had hoped for and should have valued. On the contrary, his austere face was even more severe than usual as he commented upon the things that I had done and the things that I had not.

definitions.affable: friendly and easy to talk to

rule: 'Austere' means stern. The face is 'even more severe than usual', and Holmes does not give even 'curt praise'.

passage: It would be an overstatement to say that he was shocked or even excited by the amazing announcement. Without having a tinge of cruelty in his singular composition, he was undoubtedly callous from long overstimulation. Yet, if his emotions were dulled, his intellectual perceptions were exceedingly active.
rule: 'Callous' means unfeeling. He is not 'shocked or even excited' by the news, and the passage says 'his emotions were dulled'.

why: Only polarity ('lenient', 'mild') points to it; plausible punishments like retribution also fit.
Too little context for what kind of reasons they are.

passage: "I don't know that anything she is accused of is really worse than what you have yourself admitted, that you have tried to ruin a defenceless girl who was under your roof. Some of you rich men have to be taught that all the world cannot be bribed into condoning your offences."

definitions.disparaging: speaking of as having little worth

rule: 'Condoning' means excusing or overlooking. A bribe could buy someone's tolerance of 'your offences', but it could not buy their criticism of them.
why: cut after the blind test
Other verbs like ascertained or deduced also fit what the passage describes.
Clue is weak ('traces') and the passage mentions blood on a knife.

passage: This, however, is the readiest and, since fortune has put it into our hands, I should be culpable if I neglected it. It has, however, prevented the case from becoming the pretty little intellectual problem which it at one time promised to be.

definitions.exemplary: serving as a model of good conduct

rule: 'Culpable' means deserving blame. 'Fortune has put it into our hands', so he would be at fault 'if I neglected it'.
why: cut after the blind test

passage: We were ushered through the magnificent Elizabethan doorway and into his Grace’s study. There we found Mr. James Wilder, demure and courtly, but with some trace of that wild terror of the night before still lurking in his furtive eyes and in his twitching features.
rule: 'Demure' means quiet and modest. It goes with 'courtly', and the word 'but' leads to a hint of 'wild terror' underneath.

passage: Seldom have I seen him so utterly despondent. He had been uneasy during all our journey from town, and I had observed that he had turned over the morning papers with anxious attention, but now this sudden realization of his worst fears left him in a blank melancholy.
rule: 'Despondent' means deeply discouraged. His worst fears came true and left him in 'a blank melancholy'.

why: No clue in the passage about the condition of the opening.
Frantic arrival does not rule out neat dress, so wrong choices could fit.
Wrong choices would be rejected only by grammar, not by meaning.
Passage does not separate eccentric from erratic or odd.

passage: That very night he started off all alone to prepare for the attempt. It was daylight before he returned from his reconnaissance. Next day he interviewed his two subordinates, Manders and Reilly, reckless youngsters who were as elated as if it were a deer-hunt.
rule: 'Elated' means thrilled. The youngsters are 'reckless' and treat the job 'as if' it were a fun hunt, so they are excited, not afraid.

why: Little context for what makes the reputation questionable.

passage: Both men were total abstainers, and behaved in all ways as exemplary members of the society, with the one simple exception that they were assassins who had often proved themselves to be most capable instruments for this association of murder.

definitions.exemplary: serving as a model of good conduct

rule: 'Exemplary' means a model of good behavior. They were 'total abstainers' who behaved well 'in all ways', and only 'the one simple exception' spoils it.

why: Other fussy or complaining words like querulous also fit the blank.

passage: Had he appeared surprised at his own arrest, or feigned indignation at it, I should have looked upon it as highly suspicious, because such surprise or anger would not be natural under the circumstances, and yet might appear to be the best policy to a scheming man.

definitions.relinquished: gave up or let go of

rule: 'Feigned' means pretended. The clause 'such surprise or anger would not be natural' shows that showing it would be an act.

passage: A heavy step was heard upon the stairs, and an instant later there entered a tall, ruddy, clean-shaven gentleman, whose clear eyes and florid cheeks told of a life led far from the fogs of Baker Street.
rule: 'Florid' means reddish and healthy looking. The man is 'ruddy' with 'clear eyes', which fits a life led 'far from the fogs of Baker Street'.

passage: In broken words he explained that he had no notion what had occurred to him, save that terrific pangs had suddenly shot through him, and that it had taken all his fortitude to reach the bank.
rule: 'Fortitude' means strength in the face of suffering. 'Terrific pangs' of pain made reaching the bank a test of endurance.

passage: The vicar, being a bachelor, was glad to come to such an arrangement, though he had little in common with his lodger, who was a thin, dark, spectacled man, with a stoop which gave the impression of actual, physical deformity. I remember that during our short visit we found the vicar garrulous, but his lodger strangely reticent, a sad-faced, introspective man, sitting with averted eyes, brooding apparently upon his own affairs.
rule: 'Garrulous' means talkative. The word 'but' sets up a contrast with the lodger, who was 'strangely reticent'.

why: Reproach or reprisal fit the blank about as well as hindrance.

passage: When I thought of the heavy rains and looked at the gaping roof I understood how strong and immutable must be the purpose which had kept him in that inhospitable abode. Was he our malignant enemy, or was he by chance our guardian angel?

definitions.capricious: given to sudden changes of mind

rule: 'Immutable' means unchanging. The purpose was 'strong' enough to keep him in a miserable hut through bad weather, so it never wavered.

passage: The love which had sprung up in his heart was not the sudden, changeable fancy of a boy, but rather the wild, fierce passion of a man of strong will and imperious temper. He had been accustomed to succeed in all that he undertook.
rule: 'Imperious' means bossy and commanding. It matches 'strong will', and it is the opposite of the 'changeable' fancy of a boy.

passage: We will now suppose that as he went to the theatre with the young lady he suddenly, in the fog, caught a glimpse of this same agent going in the direction of the office. He was an impetuous man, quick in his decisions. Everything gave way to his duty.

definitions.irresolute: unable to make up one's mind

rule: 'Impetuous' means acting fast on impulse. The next phrases say he was 'quick in his decisions' and that everything 'gave way to his duty'.

why: Archaic sense and no real clue in the passage.
Manner is described, not explained; clue is too vague.

passage: The moment that Hilton Cubitt’s broad back had disappeared through the door my comrade rushed to the table, laid out all the slips of paper containing dancing men in front of him, and threw himself into an intricate and elaborate calculation.

definitions.perfunctory: done with little care or effort

rule: 'Intricate' means complicated. It is paired with 'elaborate', and he 'threw himself into' it, so it was no quick or simple job.

why: Graphic scene (a mangled body) and weak clue for the word.

passage: Our visitor glanced with some apparent surprise at the languid, lounging figure of the man who had been no doubt depicted to him as the most incisive reasoner and most energetic agent in Europe. Holmes slowly reopened his eyes and looked impatiently at his gigantic client.

definitions.restive: restless and unable to stay still

rule: 'Languid' means slow and relaxed. The man is 'lounging' and only 'slowly' reopens his eyes, which surprises a visitor who expected an 'energetic' agent.

passage: This matter cuts very deep, and though I have not finally made up my mind whether it is a benevolent or a malevolent agency which is in touch with us, I am conscious always of power and design.
rule: 'Malevolent' means wishing harm. The phrase 'benevolent or a' sets up the opposite of 'benevolent', which means kind.

why: Passage does not separate morose from silent or disappointed; one candidate is violent.

passage: It has, however, prevented the case from becoming the pretty little intellectual problem which it at one time promised to be. There might have been some credit to be gained out of it, but for this too palpable clue.”

definitions.palpable: so obvious it is easy to notice

rule: 'Palpable' means obvious. The clue stopped the case from being an 'intellectual problem', so it must have given the answer away.
why: cut after the blind test
Other hard or risky words like arduous fit the blank equally well.

passage: “The London criminal is certainly a dull fellow,” said he in the querulous voice of the sportsman whose game has failed him. “Look out this window, Watson. See how the figures loom up, are dimly seen, and then blend once more into the cloud-bank.
rule: 'Querulous' means complaining. He calls the criminal 'a dull fellow' and sounds like a sportsman whose 'game has failed him'.

why: Metaphor depends on the story and wrong choices like ominous could fit.

passage: That trick of his of breaking in on his friends’ thoughts with an apropos remark after a quarter of an hour’s silence is really very showy and superficial. He had some analytical genius, no doubt; but he was by no means such a phenomenon as Poe appeared to imagine.”
rule: 'Superficial' means shallow. It matches 'showy', and the speaker adds that the man was 'by no means' a phenomenon.

passage: As we drove away I stole a glance back, and I still seem to see that little group on the step, the two graceful, clinging figures, the half-opened door, the hall-light shining through stained glass, the barometer, and the bright stair-rods. It was soothing to catch even that passing glimpse of a tranquil English home in the midst of the wild, dark business which had absorbed us.
rule: 'Tranquil' means peaceful. The glimpse was 'soothing' and is set against the 'wild, dark business' of the case.

why: No clue about what the reporter does that makes him ubiquitous.
Old age clue also fits words like decrepit; weak distinction.

passage: His handsome face was distorted with a spasm of despair, and his hands tore at his hair. For a moment we caught a glimpse of the natural man, impulsive, ardent, keenly sensitive. The next the aristocratic mask was replaced, and the gentle voice had returned.
rule: 'Ardent' means passionate. It sits in a list with 'impulsive' and 'keenly sensitive', which describe the 'natural man' under the cool mask.

passage: The swarthy giant glared at him, and his hairy paw closed for an instant round the glass as though he would hurl it at the head of his companion. Then he laughed in his loud, boisterous, insincere fashion.
rule: 'Boisterous' means loud and rowdy. It comes right after 'loud' in the list describing his laugh.

passage: My friend’s temper had not improved since he had been deprived of the congenial surroundings of Baker Street. Without his scrapbooks, his chemicals, and his homely untidiness, he was an uncomfortable man. He shrugged his shoulders in ungracious acquiescence, while our visitor in hurried words and with much excitable gesticulation poured forth his story.

definitions.congenial: pleasant and well suited to him

rule: 'Congenial' means pleasant and comfortable for him. Without his 'scrapbooks' and 'homely untidiness' he became 'uncomfortable'.

why: Unusual sense (a thicket) and the word is not used as a modern student expects.
Passage gives no real clue to the manner's quality beyond 'hostile'.
Clues are vague and sullen or hostile would fit as well.

passage: “I confess,” said he, “that any theories which I had formed from the newspaper reports were entirely erroneous. And yet there were indications there, had they not been overlaid by other details which concealed their true import.
rule: 'Erroneous' means mistaken. He says 'I confess' and then explains that real clues had been 'overlaid', so his theories were wrong.

passage: He was well dressed, but his brilliant necktie, shining pin, and glittering rings were flamboyant in their effect. As the door closed behind him he looked round him with fierce, startled eyes, like one who suspects a trap at every turn.
rule: 'Flamboyant' means showy. The 'brilliant necktie', 'shining pin', and 'glittering rings' all draw the eye.

passage: Stanley Hopkins led us first to the house, where he introduced us to a haggard, grey-haired woman, the widow of the murdered man, whose gaunt and deep-lined face, with the furtive look of terror in the depths of her red-rimmed eyes, told of the years of hardship and ill-usage which she had endured.
rule: 'Gaunt' means thin and worn looking. She is 'haggard' and her face tells of 'years of hardship and ill-usage'.

why: Passage gives no explanation of why the burglary was not haphazard.
Intrinsic or natural would fit equally and distractors are not clearly contradicted.

passage: “Well, really, it can hardly be described as otherwise,” said Sherlock Holmes, smiling at my surprise. “The proof of its intrinsic simplicity is, that without any help save a few very ordinary deductions I was able to lay my hand upon the criminal within three days.”

definitions.intrinsic: belonging naturally to the thing itself

rule: 'Intrinsic' means built in. He proves the case was truly simple because 'very ordinary deductions' solved it in three days.
why: cut after the blind test

passage: The intelligence with which Lestrade greeted us was so momentous and so unexpected, that we were all three fairly dumfoundered. Gregson sprang out of his chair and upset the remainder of his whiskey and water.

definitions.innocuous: harmless and not likely to offend

rule: 'Momentous' means very important. It is paired with 'unexpected', and the news left the men 'dumfoundered'.

passage: There was a sharp snick as the electric light was turned on. The door closed once more, and the pungent reek of a strong cigar was borne to our nostrils. Then the footsteps continued backward and forward, backward and forward, within a few yards of us.

definitions.insipid: bland and lacking flavor or smell

rule: 'Pungent' means sharp and strong smelling. The words 'reek' and 'strong cigar' show the smell was powerful.

why: No clue in any passage to suggest the color of the face.

passage: You shave every morning, and in this season you shave by the sunlight; but since your shaving is less and less complete as we get farther back on the left side, until it becomes positively slovenly as we get round the angle of the jaw, it is surely very clear that that side is less illuminated than the other.
rule: 'Slovenly' means sloppy. His shaving is 'less and less complete' on the dark side, so it ends up careless.

passage: Her visit was, I remember, extremely unwelcome to Holmes, for he was immersed at the moment in a very abstruse and complicated problem concerning the peculiar persecution to which John Vincent Harden, the well-known tobacco millionaire, had been subjected.

definitions.abstruse: hard to understand because deep or obscure
definitions.superficial: shallow, concerned only with the surface

rule: "Abstruse" means hard to understand. The problem is "complicated," Holmes is "immersed" in it, and it involves a "peculiar persecution," so it is not ordinary, silly, or shallow.

why: unclear which sense; berate or warn would both fit

passage: Our prisoner’s furious resistance did not apparently indicate any ferocity in his disposition towards ourselves, for on finding himself powerless, he smiled in an affable manner, and expressed his hopes that he had not hurt any of us in the scuffle.

definitions.affable: friendly and easy to talk to

rule: "Affable" means friendly. The prisoner "smiled" and "expressed his hopes that he had not hurt any of us," which is the opposite of gloomy, quarrelsome, or curt.

passage: Murdoch was the mathematical coach at the establishment, a tall, dark, thin man, so taciturn and aloof that none can be said to have been his friend. He seemed to live in some high, abstract region of surds and conic sections with little to connect him with ordinary life.

definitions.aloof: distant and unwilling to join others
definitions.convivial: cheerful and fond of lively company

rule: "Aloof" means distant and cold toward others. He was "taciturn and aloof" so that "none can be said to have been his friend," and a sociable or cheerful man would have had friends.

why: passage clue too weak to rule out judicious type choices

passage: I naturally began by examining the roadway, and there, as I have already explained to you, I saw clearly the marks of a cab, which, I ascertained by inquiry, must have been there during the night.
rule: "Ascertained" means found out for sure. The cab marks were learned "by inquiry," which means asking people, not guessing, demanding, or repeating.
why: cut after the blind test

passage: As he stood by the desolate fire, he felt that the only one thing which could assuage his grief would be thorough and complete retribution, brought by his own hand upon his enemies. His strong will and untiring energy should, he determined, be devoted to that one end.
rule: "Assuage" means to ease or soothe. He is in "grief" and sees "thorough and complete retribution" as the only cure, so the word must mean relieve, not make worse.

passage: I might spoil my own game, and even be ordered off the premises, if I were too audacious, for I was still conscious that I was being watched. Therefore, I strolled back to the house and waited for night before I went on with my inquiry.

definitions.audacious: bold and willing to take risks

rule: "Audacious" means bold. Being "too audacious" could "spoil my own game" and get him "ordered off the premises," while being too careful or shy would not.

passage: His broad black hat, his baggy trousers, his white tie, his sympathetic smile, and general look of peering and benevolent curiosity were such as Mr. John Hare alone could have equalled. It was not merely that Holmes changed his costume.

definitions.supercilious: acting superior and looking down on others

rule: "Benevolent" means kindly. It goes with his "sympathetic smile," so a mocking, spiteful, or snobbish look would not fit.

passage: “I begin to think, Watson,” said Holmes, “that I make a mistake in explaining. ‘Omne ignotum pro magnifico,’ you know, and my poor little reputation, such as it is, will suffer shipwreck if I am so candid.

definitions.candid: open and honest in what one says
definitions.reticent: unwilling to speak openly or share
definitions.evasive: avoiding a direct answer on purpose

rule: "Candid" means frank and open. Holmes says he "makes a mistake in explaining," so being "so candid" means telling everything openly, not holding back.
why: cut after the blind test

passage: Learn then from this story not to fear the fruits of the past, but rather to be circumspect in the future, that those foul passions whereby our family has suffered so grievously may not again be loosed to our undoing.

definitions.complacent: smugly satisfied and unaware of danger

rule: "Circumspect" means careful and cautious. The writer wants this "that those foul passions" may "not again be loosed," which calls for caution, not rashness, smugness, or fearlessness.

why: depends on unstated earlier hostility
old fashioned sense of confuse X with Y
other nouns like calamities fit equally
refute reading also fits without plot knowledge

passage: Yet when I think of him in cold blood, far away from the glamour of his presence, I am convinced from his cynical speech and the look which I have caught in his eyes that he is one who should be deeply distrusted.

definitions.cynical: distrustful and sneering about people's motives

rule: "Cynical" means scornfully distrustful. His "cynical speech" and the look in his eyes show "he is one who should be deeply distrusted," so a warm, innocent, or sincere way of speaking would not fit.

why: other reactions equally plausible in the passage
circuitous would be a synonym and others not contradicted

passage: It was at such moments that for an instant he ceased to be a reasoning machine, and betrayed his human love for admiration and applause. The same singularly proud and reserved nature which turned away with disdain from popular notoriety was capable of being moved to its depths by spontaneous wonder and praise from a friend.

definitions.disdain: scornful dislike for something seen as unworthy
definitions.trepidation: nervous fear about what may happen

rule: "Disdain" means scorn. His nature was "singularly proud and reserved," and the sentence contrasts this with his love of "admiration and applause," so he turned away from notoriety scornfully.

passage: Stand at the window here. Was ever such a dreary, dismal, unprofitable world? See how the yellow fog swirls down the street and drifts across the dun-coloured houses. What could be more hopelessly prosaic and material?

definitions.jovial: cheerful and full of good humor

rule: "Dismal" means gloomy. It sits in the list "dreary, dismal, unprofitable" and is followed by "yellow fog," so a peaceful, rich, or cheerful world would not fit.

why: hesitant glance not clearly decided by passage
wrong choices unnatural or synonyms

passage: “I think that I may go so far as to say, Watson, that I have not lived wholly in vain,” he remarked. “If my record were closed to-night I could still survey it with equanimity. The air of London is the sweeter for my presence.

definitions.equanimity: calm and steady temper, especially under pressure
definitions.remorse: deep regret and guilt over a wrong
definitions.contempt: scorn for something seen as worthless

rule: "Equanimity" means calm. Holmes says he "has not lived wholly in vain" and that London is "sweeter for my presence," so he could look back on his life calmly, not with regret, fear, or scorn.

passage: I might have rebelled against these exasperating solos had it not been that he usually terminated them by playing in quick succession a whole series of my favourite airs as a slight compensation for the trial upon my patience.

definitions.soporific: tending to make people feel sleepy

rule: "Exasperating" means extremely irritating. He "might have rebelled" against the solos, and the later tunes were "compensation for the trial upon my patience," so the solos annoyed him.

passage: On the contrary, I can never recollect having seen him in such exuberant spirits. Again and again he recurred to the fact that if he could be assured that society was freed from Professor Moriarty he would cheerfully bring his own career to a conclusion.
rule: "Exuberant" means joyfully high spirited. Holmes says he would "cheerfully" end his career if Moriarty were gone, so his "spirits" were happy, not gloomy or thoughtful.
why: cut after the blind test
weak clue

passage: For myself, I confess that I had now conceived the utmost horror of the man, not only for this cold-blooded business in which he had been concerned, but even more for the somewhat flippant and careless way in which he narrated it.

definitions.flippant: treating serious matters without proper respect

rule: "Flippant" means not serious enough about a serious matter. It is paired with "careless" and set against a "cold-blooded business," so a respectful, careful, or solemn way of telling the story does not fit.

passage: The square, massive house, with its black, empty windows and high, bare walls, towered up, sad and forlorn, behind us. Our course led right across the grounds, in and out among the trenches and pits with which they were scarred and intersected.

definitions.jaunty: cheerful and self confident in manner

rule: "Forlorn" means sad and abandoned. The house has "black, empty windows and high, bare walls" and is called "sad," so cheerful or luxurious words do not fit.

passage: I expect those cries about a monster, of which our visitor has spoken, were nocturnal reminiscences of the dear departed. However, our speculations are futile until we have all the facts. There is a cold partridge on the sideboard, Watson, and a bottle of Montrachet.

definitions.futile: useless and unable to produce results
definitions.judicious: showing good sense and sound judgment

rule: "Futile" means pointless. Holmes says the speculations are this "until we have all the facts," so guessing without facts is useless rather than convincing, wise, or sharp.

passage: Anyone could pick him at once as gregarious in his habits and communicative in his nature, with a quick wit and a ready smile. And yet the man who studied him more closely might discern a certain firmness of jaw and grim tightness about the lips which would warn him that there were depths beyond, and that this pleasant, brown-haired young Irishman might conceivably leave his mark for good or evil upon any society to which he was introduced.
rule: "Gregarious" means sociable. He is "communicative" with "a quick wit and a ready smile," so a loner, a silent man, or a cold one would not fit.

why: passage does not signal humiliation

passage: The carriage stopped, the doctor alighted, walked swiftly back to where I had also halted, and told me in an excellent sardonic fashion that he feared the road was narrow, and that he hoped his carriage did not impede the passage of my bicycle.

definitions.impede: to slow down or block progress

rule: "Impede" means to block or hinder. The doctor says he "feared the road was narrow," and his sardonic hope is that the carriage did not get in the bicycle's way.

why: clue too weak

passage: He imagined that some secret society, some implacable organization, was on Douglas’s track, which would never rest until it killed him. Some remarks of his had given him this idea; though he had never told him what the society was, nor how he had come to offend it.
rule: "Implacable" means relentless and impossible to appease. The organization "would never rest until it killed him," so it is not peaceful, generous, or harmless.

passage: No doubt the object of our journey was to catch him in the very act, and I could not but admire the cunning with which my friend had inserted a wrong clue in the evening paper, so as to give the fellow the idea that he could continue his scheme with impunity.

definitions.trepidation: fearful anxiety about what may come
definitions.remorse: deep regret and guilt over a wrong

rule: "Impunity" means without fear of being punished. Holmes planted a "wrong clue" to make the criminal believe he could "continue his scheme" safely, not with fear, regret, or shyness.

passage: And all this with such a sneering, leering, insolent face that I would have knocked him down twenty times over if he had been a man of my own age. I tell you, Holmes, I have had to keep a tight hold upon myself all this time; and now I am asking myself whether, if I had let myself go a little more, I might not have been a wiser man.
rule: "Insolent" means rude and disrespectful. It joins "sneering, leering," and the speaker says he "would have knocked him down twenty times over," so the face was not modest, kind, or shy.

passage: If Garcia could do whatever he had to do and be back by the hour mentioned he had evidently a powerful reply to any accusation. Here was this irreproachable Englishman ready to swear in any court of law that the accused was in the house all the time. It was an insurance against the worst.”

definitions.irreproachable: blameless, with no fault to criticize

rule: "Irreproachable" means blameless. The man is a witness "ready to swear in any court of law," an "insurance against the worst," so he must be trusted, not notorious, doubtful, or wicked.

why: depends on unstated look on his face

passage: A change had come over Holmes’s manner. He had lost his listless expression, and again I saw an alert light of interest in his keen, deep-set eyes. He raised the cork and examined it minutely.
rule: "Listless" means lacking energy. He "lost" that look and "again" showed "an alert light of interest," so it must be the opposite of alert and eager.

passage: You have called, as I understand, to malign my fiancé, Baron Gruner. It is only by my father's request that I see you at all, and I warn you in advance that anything you can say could not possibly have the slightest effect upon my mind.'

definitions.malign: to speak harmful or evil words about

rule: "Malign" means to speak ill of. She warns that anything the visitor says "could not possibly have the slightest effect upon my mind," which only makes sense if he came to attack her fiance.

passage: To tell the truth, my desire to fetch a doctor had somewhat weakened, for poor Holmes was so obviously delirious that it seemed dangerous to leave him. However, he was as eager now to consult the person named as he had been obstinate in refusing.

definitions.compliant: willing to go along with others

rule: "Vacuous" means empty of thought. His expression made Jimmy's face look "quite intelligent by contrast," so Gerald's face must look blank, not clever, thoughtful, or learned.

passage: Virginia said nothing. For the first time she felt afraid of this stolid man with the expressionless face. She understood what Anthony had meant when he said there were no flies on Superintendent Battle.
rule: "Stolid" means calm and showing little emotion. The man has an "expressionless face," so he cannot be bubbly, jolly, or quick to anger.

passage: “I must say, Mr. Cade,” he said pompously, “that I consider your action in that matter highly reprehensible. If the slightest hitch had occurred in your plans, one of our national possessions might have disappeared beyond the hope of recovery.
rule: "Reprehensible" means deserving blame. He starts "I must say" and then warns that "the slightest hitch" could have lost a national treasure, so he is criticizing Mr. Cade, not praising a careful or clever plan.

passage: Remembering Poirot’s unaccountable insistence on the footprints in the flower beds, I scrutinized him narrowly as he gave his evidence. Either he had nothing to do with the crime or he was a consummate actor.
rule: "Scrutinized" means examined very closely. The speaker watches him "narrowly as he gave his evidence" and then judges whether he is guilty or "a consummate actor," so he is studying him, not scolding or soothing him.

passage: "Frightfully tiring, full of all the most depressing virtues like sobriety and punctuality. I don't know which are the worst, powerful personalities or earnest politicians. I do so prefer the cheerful inefficient."
rule: "Earnest" means serious and sincere. She complains about "depressing virtues like sobriety and punctuality" and prefers "the cheerful inefficient," so the politicians she dislikes must be solemn, not silly or lazy.

passage: "A white crystalline powder, that's what it is," said Jimmy. "And to any reader of detective fiction those words are both familiar and suggestive. Of course, if it turns out to be a new kind of patent tooth-powder, I shall be chagrined and annoyed."

definitions.chagrined: feeling disappointed and a little embarrassed
definitions.mollified: calmed down and made less angry

rule: "Chagrined" means disappointed and embarrassed. He hopes the powder is something exciting, and if it is only "tooth-powder" he will feel "annoyed," so he would not be joyful, proved right, or soothed.

why: fixed phrase, or the form is a different word and wrong choices fit as well

passage: Every now and then she dabbed her eyes with a handkerchief. Madge was resolute and alert, her feelings fully under control by now. Mrs. Graham was composed, as always, her face grave and impassive. The tragedy seemed to have affected her son more keenly than anyone.

definitions.distraught: deeply upset and unable to think clearly

rule: "Resolute" means firm and determined. Madge is also "alert," with "her feelings fully under control," so she is steady, not upset, drained of energy, or hopeless.

why: wrong choices would be given away by grammar rather than meaning

passage: "You're rather a big bug socially, aren't you?" he asked, with a diffident candor that made it impossible to take offense. "I mean you know all the duchesses and earls and countesses and things."

definitions.presumptuous: overstepping what is proper or polite

rule: "Diffident" means shy and modest. His candor "made it impossible to take offense," so it was gentle and unsure, not bold, rude, or pushy.

passage: It is odd how, when you have a secret belief of your own which you do not wish to acknowledge, the voicing of it by some one else will rouse you to a fury of denial. I burst immediately into indignant speech.

definitions.conciliatory: trying to calm and win over

rule: "Indignant" means angry at something unfair. The speaker is roused "to a fury of denial" and "burst" into speech, so the words were angry, not cheerful, soothing, or calm.
